analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare HMOs to offer seniors the option to see doctors outside the plan network.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with 27 House members signed on, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health maintenance organizations serving Medicare patients to offer, at enrollment, a plan covering services from doctors outside the HMO's contracted network. Seniors locked into a closed network would gain the choice to go outside it for covered care. It applied to Medicare contracts beginning in 1998. The House never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare HMOs that cover care only through the plan's own contracted network of doctors and hospitals. Under the bill, those plans would have to offer an out-of-network coverage option at the time of enrollment, so a beneficiary who wanted a specific specialist or hospital not in the plan could still get covered care.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare HMOs would have to offer members, at enrollment, a plan that covers covered services not furnished through the plan's contracted provider network, giving seniors a choice beyond the HMO's own doctors [S2] [S3].
The requirement would attach to Medicare's contracts with these organizations and take effect for contract years beginning in 1998 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: HMOs participating in Medicare would bear the cost of building and offering an out-of-network coverage option, and part of that cost would likely flow into plan premiums or Medicare payments to the plans. Plans that found the mandate uneconomical could have scaled back their Medicare offerings, reducing the number of HMO options available to seniors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare HMOs and Medicare plans' premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates an additional coverage option but does not specify how out-of-network services would be paid for, so plans could offset the cost through higher premiums, higher cost-sharing on the out-of-network option, or by leaving the Medicare market entirely, which would reduce seniors' choices [S2] [S3].

The out-of-network option would only be offered at the time of enrollment, so a beneficiary whose doctor left the network mid-year could not switch to the out-of-network plan until the next enrollment period [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: Medicare HMOs of that era often covered care only within a closed network, leaving enrollees with no covered access to outside doctors. The fix was narrow and light on detail — it did not specify benefit levels or financing for the out-of-network option, and plans could have passed costs to enrollees or exited the Medicare market. On balance it was a modest pro-patient mandate whose main cost fell on the managed care industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Commerce committees, sent to subcommittees a week later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Coburn introduced the bill on January 21, 1997, with 21 other original cosponsors from both parties [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and also to the Commerce Committee on the day of introduction [S1] [S5].
On January 27, 1997, it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill attracted 26 additional cosponsors — 18 Republicans, 7 Democrats, and 1 Independent — but died in committee at the end of the 105th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare HMOs and the managed care industry came out ahead: no out-of-network coverage mandate was ever imposed on their Medicare contracts. Seniors in closed-network HMO plans gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare HMOs and managed care insurers

for.name: Tom Coburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring Medicare HMOs to offer out-of-network coverage options to enrollees.

for.name: 26 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral and sent it to the Health and Environment Subcommittee, where it stalled without action.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 18 Republicans, 7 Democrats, and 1 Independent among the 26 cosponsors — and there was no recorded vote, so no party split on the merits ever appeared.

industries.industry: HMOs and managed care insurers in Medicare
industries.note: The bill would have forced Medicare HMOs to build and offer an out-of-network coverage option, expanding care access at the plans' expense. Industry interest ran against the beneficiary interest the bill served.
Doctors and hospitals not contracted with a senior's HMO could treat that senior with coverage, expanding their pool of potential Medicare patients. Seniors would benefit from the same access.
